explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The LORD says, "For I have chosen him, so that he will command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD by doing what is right and just…" (Genesis 18:19). So Abraham's chosen to hand something down, and it starts at home. I like that. The best recipes get passed down the same way, standing at the counter.

This one is actually true, friend. The LORD says, "For I have chosen him, so that he will command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD by doing what is right and just…" (Genesis 18:19). The reason He gives is that Abraham will pass the way of the LORD down to his household. Good news is, it's a real easy one to remember next time.

explanations.answer: Go down and see if their actions fit the outcry
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD says, "I will go down to see if their actions fully justify the outcry that has reached Me. If not, I will find out." (Genesis 18:21). He says He will go down and see. Nobody rushes this one, and I think that matters.

explanations.answer: Wipe out both cities before the sun goes down
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The LORD doesn't say a word about the sun going down. He says, "I will go down to see if their actions fully justify the outcry that has reached Me. If not, I will find out." (Genesis 18:21). So the plan is to go down and see for Himself. That's a pretty big difference from a countdown clock.

explanations.answer: Leave the two cities alone until next year
explanations.explanation: Close to the calendar, but no, baker. The LORD gives no timeline like that. He says, "I will go down to see if their actions fully justify the outcry that has reached Me. If not, I will find out." (Genesis 18:21). He isn't putting it off. He's going to see it for Himself.

explanations.answer: Will You really sweep away the righteous with the wicked
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker! Abraham asks, "Will You really sweep away the righteous with the wicked?" (Genesis 18:23). He steps forward to say it, too. Notice he doesn't ask to be let off. He asks about the righteous people who might be in that city.

explanations.answer: Will You really send a warning to the wicked first
explanations.explanation: Good guess, friend, but that's not what Abraham asks. He says, "Will You really sweep away the righteous with the wicked?" (Genesis 18:23). His question is about the righteous being swept away alongside the wicked. A warning never comes up in his words.

explanations.answer: Will You really let me walk down with the two men
explanations.explanation: Nope, baker. Abraham stays put. The two men go toward Sodom, but he "remained standing before the LORD" (Genesis 18:22). Then he asks, "Will You really sweep away the righteous with the wicked?" (Genesis 18:23). He's not asking to go anywhere. He's asking a question.

explanations.answer: The Judge of all the earth
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. Abraham says, "Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?" (Genesis 18:25). Think about why that title fits. He's asking about judging, so he calls the LORD the Judge. He also says, "Far be it from You!" twice, which tells me he means every word.

That's a real title, friend, but it's not the one Abraham uses here. "The Shepherd of Israel" shows up in Psalm 80:1. Abraham says, "Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?" (Genesis 18:25). He's talking about right and wrong treatment, so he picks the title that matches.

Nice title, baker, but Abraham doesn't use it. "The King of glory" comes from Psalm 24:7. Abraham says, "Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?" (Genesis 18:25). His question is about judging, so the title is Judge.

Yes, baker! The LORD says, "If I find fifty righteous ones within the city of Sodom, on their account I will spare the whole place." (Genesis 18:26). Spare the WHOLE place, mind you. Abraham asked about fifty righteous people, and the answer covers everybody else there too.

I see why you'd think it, friend, but warn isn't the word. The LORD says, "If I find fifty righteous ones within the city of Sodom, on their account I will spare the whole place." (Genesis 18:26). He says spare. And it covers the whole place, not just the fifty.

Tricky one, baker, since Abraham just called Him the Judge. But the LORD's word here is spare. He says, "If I find fifty righteous ones within the city of Sodom, on their account I will spare the whole place." (Genesis 18:26). The whole place is spared on account of the fifty.

Yes, baker. Abraham asks, "suppose the fifty righteous ones lack five. Will You destroy the whole city for the lack of five?" and the LORD replies, "If I find forty-five there, I will not destroy it." (Genesis 18:28). Five short, and the answer is still no destruction. Abraham is just getting warmed up.

Other way around, friend. Abraham asks about the fifty lacking five, and the LORD replies, "If I find forty-five there, I will not destroy it." (Genesis 18:28). So forty-five is enough. The answer is a yes to Abraham.

Not this time, baker. Abraham says, "Suppose thirty are found there?" and the LORD replies, "If I find thirty there, I will not do it." (Genesis 18:30). Thirty is enough to spare the city. So the statement on the card has it backwards.

You've got it, baker. Abraham asks, "Suppose thirty are found there?" and the LORD replies, "If I find thirty there, I will not do it." (Genesis 18:30). He says thirty is enough, not that it falls short. Abraham asked and the answer was yes again.

That's it, baker! Abraham says, "Now that I have ventured to speak to the Lord, suppose twenty are found there?" (Genesis 18:31). Each time he asks, the number drops. And each time, the answer is the same: no destruction. The LORD answers, "On account of the twenty, I will not destroy it."
Close, friend, but he skips right past it. After thirty, Abraham says, "suppose twenty are found there?" (Genesis 18:31). He goes down by ten this time. Twenty-five never comes up.

Not yet, baker. Fifteen never comes up in this conversation. After thirty, Abraham says, "suppose twenty are found there?" (Genesis 18:31). The LORD answers, "On account of the twenty, I will not destroy it."

Right, baker. Abraham says, "May the Lord not be angry, but let me speak once more. Suppose ten are found there?" (Genesis 18:32). And the LORD answers, "On account of the ten, I will not destroy it." Ten is where Abraham stops asking.

Good thinking, friend, but fifteen isn't a number Abraham uses. He says, "let me speak once more. Suppose ten are found there?" (Genesis 18:32). It's the lowest number in the whole conversation. Ten is where he lands.

I get it, baker. Five did come up earlier, when Abraham said fifty lacks five (Genesis 18:28). But this time, he says, "let me speak once more. Suppose ten are found there?" (Genesis 18:32). Ten is his last number.

explanations.answer: The LORD departs and Abraham returns home
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. "When the LORD had finished speaking with Abraham, He departed, and Abraham returned home." (Genesis 18:33). The conversation ends, and Abraham goes back home. The text doesn't say what Abraham was thinking on that walk. I'd bet it was a quiet one.

explanations.answer: Abraham follows the two men toward Sodom
explanations.explanation: No, friend. The two men went toward Sodom earlier (Genesis 18:22). At the end, "When the LORD had finished speaking with Abraham, He departed, and Abraham returned home." (Genesis 18:33). Abraham heads home, not to Sodom.

explanations.answer: Abraham asks about five righteous people
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. Abraham's last ask is ten, and then it's over. "When the LORD had finished speaking with Abraham, He departed, and Abraham returned home." (Genesis 18:33). So there's no question about five at the end.
